title: Two numbers that multiply to ten thousand
description: Ten thousand is four twos and four fives multiplied together. Keeping all the twos in one number and all the fives in the other gives sixteen and six hundred and twenty five, and neither ends in zero.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number that holds both a two and a five ends in zero, so the twos and fives of ten thousand must be kept apart. Watch for students who try two and five thousand, where five thousand ends in zero.

video_script.why: The child breaks ten thousand into tens, each ten into two times five, and then keeps the twos in one number and the fives in the other.
video_script.substitution: Write 10000 as four tens, each ten as 2 x 5, then collect all the twos in one number and all the fives in the other.
video_script.anchor: the number 10000 as a block, with two empty boxes joined by a times sign
video_script.payoff_line: Sixteen times six hundred and twenty five is ten thousand

final_answer.spoken: sixteen times six hundred and twenty five is ten thousand

maths_rules: 10000 = 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 and 10 = 2 x 5, so 10000 is four 2s and four 5s multiplied together
a number that has both a 2 and a 5 inside it is a multiple of 10, so it ends in 0
put all the 2s in one number: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16; put all the 5s in the other: 5 x 5 x 5 x 5 = 625
16 ends in 6 and 625 ends in 5, so neither ends in 0
1000 = 8 x 125 = (2 x 2 x 2) x (5 x 5 x 5) is the same idea with three of each
video_script.design: One idea: split the twos and the fives of ten thousand into different numbers. Callback to the split of one thousand into eight and one hundred and twenty five. Wrong idea: none is broken. The block of ten thousand stays on the board to the end.
